title: Before You Act: Five Questions That Improve Leadership Decisions
author: Kurt Mueller
source: Rookie to Pro: The Hidden Side of Leadership (Substack)
summary: Kurt Mueller argues that most leadership mistakes happen not because leaders make wrong decisions but because they move to decision before adequately understanding the situation. The article proposes five assessment questions as a pre-decision discipline. Four are fully presented: What is the Required Deliverable? (without clarity on the actual outcome needed, activity masquerades as progress); Who Depends On It? (not all stakeholders have equal dependency -- identifying who cannot succeed without your deliverable clarifies priorities); What Impact Will It Create? (leaders create value through impact, not activity -- asking how delivery helps others succeed redirects effort from internal process to external value); and What Remains Uncertain? (uncertainty doesn't disappear when ignored -- listing assumptions and verifying them is proactive, not postponement). The article frames this as a 'stakeholder impact chain': each situation runs through the five questions to produce clearer understanding, then better decisions, then greater stakeholder impact. The core reframe is from activity to impact: the measure of effective leadership is not what the leader did but whether the people who depended on the outcome were able to succeed.
points: Most leadership mistakes happen because the wrong problem is being solved -- the instinct to act immediately bypasses the prior step of understanding the situation clearly enough to know what the deliverable, dependencies, and impacts actually are.

Deliverable clarity is the first check: without knowing specifically what constitutes success (not what is plausible to do, but what the stakeholder actually needs), activity misaligns with need -- as when a leader optimizes for accuracy when the stakeholder needed timeliness.

Dependency mapping distinguishes stakeholders by degree of dependency: the prioritization question is not 'who asked?' but 'who cannot function without this?' -- a frame that clarifies triage when multiple demands compete.

Uncertainty addressed proactively is far cheaper than uncertainty revealed after a wrong decision: listing assumptions and verifying them prevents the common failure of acting on information that has already changed.

The stakeholder impact chain reframes leadership effectiveness from activity (what the leader did) to impact (whether those who depended on the outcome succeeded) -- making the quality of assessment before action the primary leadership skill.
quotes: Many leadership mistakes happen because the wrong problem is being solved. Your instinct is often to jump immediately into action. But the quality of your leadership decisions is often determined long before the decision itself. It begins with how well you assess the situation.

Without clarity about the desired outcome, activity can easily be mistaken for progress. A leader focuses on reducing errors in a report. The stakeholder actually needs the report two days earlier. The deliverable was timeliness, not accuracy.
Not all stakeholders have equal dependency. Two stakeholders request help. One would be inconvenienced without it. The other cannot complete their work without it. The priorities become clear.

Leaders create value through impact, not activity. A team spends weeks improving an internal process no stakeholder notices. Meanwhile a small improvement to customer response time would have delivered greater value.

Most leaders spend significant time discussing solutions. Fewer spend enough time understanding the situation. Yet the quality of your decision is often determined before the decision is ever made. Assess first. Then decide.
